title: AI Can Reverse Engineer Your Code. CORE License Helps Keep Its Future Open.
summary:
AI Is Changing the Rules of Software Development

For decades, software developers have faced a familiar dilemma:

Should we make our software open source, or keep it proprietary to protect our work?

Open source enables collaboration, transparency, innovation, and collective progress. But it also introduces a concern: someone can take years of community development, modify the software, and potentially turn those improvements into a closed-source product.

Artificial intelligence makes this concern even more relevant.

Today, AI can analyze enormous codebases, understand complex architectures, reconstruct functionality, translate software between programming languages, and generate alternative implementations at unprecedented speed.

Tasks that previously required months of engineering can sometimes be accelerated dramatically.

And as AI becomes more capable, the technical barriers to reproducing software will continue to decrease.

But perhaps we are asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking how to stop AI from understanding our software, shouldn't we ask how to keep software innovation open for everyone?

That is the philosophy behind the CORE License.

The Real Problem Isn't Reverse Engineering

Reverse engineering is not inherently bad.

It has legitimate purposes in security research, interoperability, education, compatibility, and software preservation.

AI-assisted reverse engineering can make these activities more accessible.

The problem arises when technology developed through open collaboration is taken in a direction that prevents the community from benefiting from future improvements.

Consider a simple scenario:

  1. A community develops an open-source software project.
  2. Hundreds of developers contribute code, improvements, bug fixes, and documentation.
  3. A company uses AI to understand and modify the project.
  4. The company develops a significantly improved version.
  5. Those improvements are kept proprietary, and the original community cannot build upon them.

The company may have created something valuable, but the shared development process has become one-directional.

The community contributes openly. The company benefits privately.

This is not necessarily unlawful under every license. Some permissive licenses explicitly allow proprietary derivatives.

But it raises an important question:

If everyone benefits from open development, why shouldn't the improvements remain open too?

Introducing the CORE License

The CORE License approaches software freedom with a simple philosophy:

Allow everyone to use, modify, distribute, and commercialize software. Keep its shared source-code evolution open.

It is not intended to prevent commercial development.

It is not intended to prohibit AI.

It is not intended to restrict who can participate.

Instead, it focuses on preserving public access to source code and contributions when covered source code is distributed.

The license grants broad permissions, including the rights to:

  • Use and copy software.
  • Modify and merge software.
  • Publish and distribute software.
  • Sublicense software.
  • Sell software and build commercial products.

Its central condition is:

All distribution of the Covered Software in Source Code Form, including any Modifications and/or Contributions must be disclosed and publicly available.

That is the essential idea.

Freedom to innovate, with an obligation to preserve openness where the license requires it.

The license also includes standard warranty and liability disclaimers.

Why This Matters in the Age of AI

AI changes the economics of software development.

Previously, understanding and modifying a large software project required substantial human effort.

Now, AI can assist with:

  • Understanding unfamiliar source code.
  • Identifying algorithms and design patterns.
  • Reconstructing software behavior.
  • Migrating applications between languages.
  • Finding performance optimizations.
  • Generating modifications and extensions.
  • Automating repetitive engineering work.

These capabilities can benefit both open-source communities and commercial organizations.

But AI also makes it easier to extract value from publicly available work without necessarily participating in the community that created it.

The CORE License proposes a different direction.

Rather than trying to stop AI from studying software, it aims to keep covered source-code development accessible.

AI can help create better software. Developers can use AI to improve existing projects. Companies can commercialize their innovations.

The goal is not to stop progress. It is to prevent openness from becoming a one-way street.

There is an important legal distinction: a license cannot automatically claim ownership of every independently developed implementation that reproduces similar functionality. Whether AI-assisted output constitutes a modification or derivative of licensed code depends on the facts and applicable law.

The CORE License's actual source-distribution condition should therefore not be confused with a universal prohibition on proprietary AI-generated implementations.

One Project, Thousands of Contributors, One Shared Future

The most powerful aspect of open source is not simply that people can read code.

It is that people can build upon one another's work.

Imagine a decentralized networking library.

One developer creates its communication protocol.

Another implements encryption.

Another improves performance.

Another develops mobile compatibility.

Another adds hardware integration.

An AI-assisted developer optimizes the entire architecture.

A company builds a commercial application around it.

Each contribution can make the underlying technology more valuable.

Now imagine this process happening across multiple projects working toward the same technological movement.

They might use different programming languages, target different platforms, or serve different industries.

Yet their development efforts can reinforce each other.

This is the real power of open development:

Innovation does not have to remain isolated inside individual organizations.

When improvements remain available to the community, every contributor can benefit from the collective progress.

A fix discovered in one implementation can inspire improvements in another.

A performance optimization can benefit thousands of applications.

A security improvement can protect an entire ecosystem.

And AI can accelerate all of it.

Why Not Simply Ban AI Reverse Engineering?

Some developers may respond to AI by introducing increasingly restrictive license conditions.

They might attempt to prohibit AI training, automated code analysis, reverse engineering, commercial usage, or particular categories of users.

But restrictions introduce complexity.

They create uncertainty about which tools developers can use and which activities are permitted.

They can also discourage legitimate innovation.

The CORE License takes a different philosophical approach.

Don't restrict who can innovate. Protect the openness of shared innovation.

Developers should be able to use the tools they want.

Businesses should be able to build products.

Researchers should be able to experiment.

AI should be able to assist software development.

The emphasis is on the availability of covered source code and its modifications when the license's distribution condition applies.

The goal is not to control how software is developed.

It is to preserve an environment where everyone can continue building.

Open Source Should Not Be Anti-Business

One of the most common misconceptions about source-sharing licenses is that they are opposed to commercial activity.

But open development and commercial success are not mutually exclusive.

A company can create value through hosting, support, customization, integration, infrastructure, reliability, expertise, and many other services.

Keeping source code open does not eliminate these opportunities.

In fact, open ecosystems can create larger markets by reducing barriers to adoption and encouraging interoperability.

The CORE License explicitly grants permission to sell copies of software.

Its philosophy is not that developers should work for free.

It is that commercial success should not require closing the source of collectively developed technology.

A business can compete on execution, service quality, innovation, and trust.

It does not necessarily need exclusive control over the underlying code.

The Difference Between Protecting Code and Protecting Collaboration

Traditional proprietary licensing often focuses on controlling access.

Who can read the source?

Who can copy it?

Who can modify it?

Who can distribute it?

The CORE philosophy shifts the emphasis.

The important question becomes:

How do we preserve the ability of future developers to build on what previous developers created?

This matters because software is rarely developed in isolation.

Modern applications depend on libraries, frameworks, protocols, standards, and infrastructure created by countless contributors.

Even seemingly independent projects often benefit from decades of publicly shared knowledge.

AI makes these connections more powerful.

It can identify relationships between technologies and help transfer ideas across programming languages, platforms, and architectures.

The opportunity is enormous.

But the benefits are greatest when improvements can flow back into the shared ecosystem.

Open source should be a continuously expanding foundation, not merely a free starting point for closed development.

What CORE License Does — and Does Not — Guarantee

It is important to distinguish the philosophy of the CORE License from the precise legal obligations in its current text.

The license explicitly requires public availability when covered software is distributed in source-code form, including modifications and contributions.

However, the current wording does not expressly establish all the obligations associated with stronger copyleft licenses.

For example, it does not explicitly require every binary-only distribution to be accompanied by source code. Nor does it explicitly address network-only services, AI training, model outputs, or independently reimplemented software.

These distinctions matter.

A license can support a philosophy without automatically enforcing every possible interpretation of that philosophy.

For CORE License, the long-term vision is straightforward:

Software should remain accessible for future development, regardless of whether its improvements come from humans, AI, individuals, or corporations.

Achieving that vision consistently requires precise licensing language and clear definitions of covered modifications and distribution obligations.

The simplicity of the license is part of its appeal, but simplicity should not come at the expense of legal clarity.

The Future of Software Is Collective

AI will continue making software easier to understand, reproduce, modify, and improve.

Trying to preserve innovation solely through technical secrecy will become increasingly difficult.

But there is another approach.

Instead of treating every new developer, company, or AI system as a potential threat, we can build ecosystems where participation creates shared value.

Where one project's success benefits another.

Where developers do not need permission to experiment.

Where commercial organizations can innovate without excluding the community.

Where AI accelerates collective progress instead of merely accelerating the creation of proprietary alternatives.

And where the source code remains a foundation for future generations.

The CORE License represents a simple principle:

Keep software open. Keep innovation free. Keep the source available for everyone to build upon.

Not by adding endless restrictions.

Not by fighting AI.

Not by preventing commercialization.

But by protecting the openness that makes collective development possible.

Final Thoughts

The greatest threat to open-source development is not that AI can understand our code.

Understanding is how innovation begins.

The greater concern is losing access to the improvements built upon shared work.

We should not fear a future where AI can reverse engineer software.

We should work toward a future where AI-assisted development strengthens the open ecosystem.

Because the real power of open source is not just making code publicly available today.

It is ensuring that tomorrow's developers can continue building on it.

And that is a future worth protecting.

สกิล Claude คืออะไร

สกิลคือชุดไฟล์คำสั่งที่เอเจนต์อ่านก่อนทำงาน ตามข้อกำหนดของ Agent Skills [16]

มันไม่ได้เพิ่มความสามารถให้โมเดลโดยตรง แต่บอกวิธีทำงานที่ถูกต้อง เช่น ต้องสร้างไฟล์อะไร ใช้เครื่องมือไหน และตรวจงานอย่างไร

ทุกครั้งที่เรียกใช้ เนื้อหาสกิลจะถูกโหลดเข้า context ของ LLM และนับเป็น token ซึ่งมีค่าใช้จ่าย

ยิ่งสกิลยาวและใช้หลายตัวพร้อมกัน ค่าใช้จ่ายก็ยิ่งสูง

ทุกครั้งที่เอเจนต์ตอบ มันคำนวณ probability ของ token ถัดไปผ่าน softmax และประมวลผล context ทั้งชุดผ่านชั้น attention ของ Transformer [15]

ในทางเทคนิค ทุก token ที่เพิ่มเข้า context ต้องผ่านชั้น attention ของโมเดล Transformer ทำให้งานคำนวณหนักขึ้น

ค่าใช้จ่ายจึงขึ้นกับจำนวน token ไม่ใช่จำนวนคำสั่งที่คุณพิมพ์

ก่อนถึงชั้น attention ข้อความถูกแปลงเป็น embedding vector แล้วคูณ matrix หลายชั้น ซึ่งเป็น linear algebra พื้นฐานของโมเดล [15]

title: Serving a stateful video world model on one RTX 4090: memory, flags and seeds in Hy-Nomas
summary:
Most open video models give you a clip and drop it. Hy-Nomas holds on to the world between calls, and that reshapes the server around it.

The model comes from Tencent Hunyuan, with weights and code under Apache-2.0 on the Hy-Nomas model card and in the Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Nomas repository. You steer it in 5-second turns, each built on the frames already made. The default launch shares one video between eight GPUs, but the authors also ship a low-memory preset for a lone RTX 4090. We tried it as published, on a 24 GB RTX 4090 on our cloud. Every figure below comes from the Hy-Nomas single-GPU research write-up.

Headline numbers: 88 to 94 seconds of GPU work per 5-second segment once warm (after the first call has loaded everything), an 18.5 GiB peak on the card, and a scene that stayed coherent for three turns.

The server is stateful, so plan in worlds

As it draws, the model writes notes on the scene and reads them before the next turn. The preset keeps only the newest few seconds of notes on the GPU and parks the rest in main memory (host RAM). Our backend, a small program between the platform's API and the model, wraps the authors' own generation service and keeps a single world resident. A request carries one turn and returns a 5-second MP4; the next one picks up where it ended.

So one GPU holds exactly one live world, for one person. Size the fleet by open worlds, not requests per second.

Host RAM is the second budget. The parked notes grew by about 5.9 GiB per segment, linearly over the three segments we ran. Our SDK example requests 64 GB of RAM, a provisioning pick rather than a measured floor. A one-minute world is twelve segments, so check the host side first.

The trap: two decode flags from the live-demo script

Decoding turns the model's internal result into video frames. The authors' live-demo script starts it while the video model still sits on the GPU:

inference.seg_ar_segment_vae_decode=true
model.vae.stable_prefix_streaming=true

On 24 GB, the pair runs out of memory. We removed both, so decoding waits until drawing is done. Status: worked around in our example, not yet reported upstream.

The hardware check that is easy to miss

The preset compiles a GPU routine (a kernel) for its decoder on NVIDIA's CUTLASS, using 8-bit numbers (FP8). It targets one GPU generation only: Ada, the RTX 4090 family. Any other generation gets an error, so an RTX 5090 or an A40 should fail, though we ran neither. The spec is "24 GB and Ada", not just "24 GB".

To find the floor, we capped memory on the same card:

Memory available Result
24 GB RTX 4090, real card works, 88 to 94 s per segment
capped at 20 GiB works over two turns, no slowdown
capped at 16 GiB fails while moving the text reader to the GPU

At 16 GiB it crashes before drawing anything, so lower resolution would not help. We have not tried a real 20 GB card, and the authors' own one-card run hit 20.53 GiB with segments longer than ours.

What to log on every turn

Of a ninety-second turn, roughly 35 seconds is drawing, roughly 9 is writing the scene notes, and the remainder goes to decoding frames and encoding the MP4. A cold first call after a restart took as long as 138 seconds. The per-stage timings in the Hy-Nomas write-up show which stage a faster turn would have to shrink.

Log per call:

  • GPU seconds per segment, warm and cold
  • peak GPU memory, which crept up each turn for reasons we did not find
  • host RAM after each segment
  • an md5 hash of each segment's video file

A seed is the fixed random number that drives generation. The same turns and seed produced byte-identical files in four runs on one machine. A bug report can ship its exact inputs and reproduce the clip. The seed also belongs to the world: an early backend answered a seedless continue turn with an HTTP 400, as the seed no longer matched. Backend 0.1.2 now keeps the seed from the first turn.

Two platform limits, both open, shaped the API: calls that wait for the answer stop at 300 seconds, so one segment per call, and messages cap at 8 MB, so the client stitches segments itself.

What the model did and did not follow

Continuity was the strength: fox, path and light survived from call to call. Steering was weak: one scene change in four landed. Flowers showed up; snow, a storm and requested actions did not. Our prompts were handwritten, without Nomas-PE, the authors' far larger prompt rewriter; whether it brings the weather is untested, like camera paths.

At roughly 18 times slower than real time, this is for sketching scenes that stay put across turns. Think rehearsal room, not stage.

Credits: the model, its single-GPU preset, its INT8 and FP8 weights and the generation service our backend wraps are the work of Tencent Hunyuan, described in their paper on arXiv. Tencent fine-tuned the decoder from PixelUMM (Wei et al., 2026) and published a Diffusers conversion built on a fork by jiaxiangc. Qwen2.5-VL-7B, from the Qwen team, reads the instructions, and NVIDIA's CUTLASS sits under the FP8 kernel. We first saw the model in a news video from AI Search. Our share: the backend, measurements, memory caps and SDK example. The per-turn table, request format, setup steps and every problem with its status are in the full Hy-Nomas test on one RTX 4090.

title: How Accurate Is Statistical Computation in JavaScript? — A Comparative Analysis: rStats.js vs. R
summary:
Introduction

When performing statistical analysis in JavaScript, one of the primary concerns is: "Can the calculation results truly be trusted?" In scenarios such as the tails of probability distributions, cases involving extremely large parameters, or instances with infinitesimal probabilities, the choice of numerical computation method can lead to significant discrepancies in the results.

To address this challenge directly, I am developing rStats.js, a statistical computation library for JavaScript. In this project, I use R as a key benchmark to continuously verify the accuracy of these statistical calculations.

In this article, I will explain the methodology used to compare rStats.js against R, as well as the level of precision I aim to achieve.

1. Automated Verification Against R 4.6.2

In rStats.js, the general policy is to compare every public-facing function against R version 4.6.2. This goes beyond simply testing a few representative input values; the test suite incorporates a diverse range of input conditions, including:

  • Typical input values
  • Extremely small probabilities (e.g., 1e-300)
  • The extreme tails of distributions
  • Boundary values ​​(e.g., 0, 1, or cases where degrees of freedom approach infinity)
  • NaN and Infinity
  • Negative values
  • Extremely large parameters

The expected values—calculated using R—are generated via dedicated R scripts and stored as JSON fixtures. Consequently, there is no need to have R installed when running the tests; the results from R are pre-saved, allowing the JavaScript test suite to verify against them.

2. Precision Standards Vary by Function Type

When evaluating the accuracy of numerical computations, applying a uniform margin of error across all functions is not appropriate. In rStats.js, the allowable margin of error is tailored to the specific nature of each calculation.

Calculation Type Relative Tolerance
Special functions, probability densities, and distribution functions 1e-14
Descriptive statistics 1e-14
Hypothesis testing 1e-12 ​​
Linear models 1e-12 ​​
Linear algebra 1e-14 – 1e-13
Numerical methods 1e-14 – 1e-15
Mixed-effects models Primarily 1e-12 – 1e-9

These values ​​are not merely design targets; they are tolerances established based on the results of running a large number of test cases.

Note that not all results can be evaluated solely by simple relative error. In cases where values ​​are close to zero or where numerical cancellation occurs, evaluation is performed using absolute error or an appropriate scale.

3. R’s Results Are Not Always Correct

This is an aspect to which we pay particular attention during the development of rStats.js.

While R is an excellent environment for statistical computing, its numerical calculations are not necessarily accurate under all conditions. In scenarios involving extremely small probabilities or exceptionally large parameter values, even R can be subject to rounding errors or loss of precision.

Therefore, if our results do not match those of R, we do not automatically assume that the error lies with rStats.js. Instead, we calculate high-precision reference values ​​when necessary to verify which result is mathematically correct.

To calculate these reference values, we primarily use the following methods:

  • Arbitrary-precision arithmetic (256–1300 bits) via Rmpfr
  • Exact rational number arithmetic via gmp
  • High-precision computation via mpmath
  • Independent verification using numerical integration or mathematically derived series

For instance, if the value of a probability distribution function does not match R’s output, but it does align with our high-precision reference value, we consider that result to be "more accurate than R." ## 4. Cases where more accurate results are returned than in R

Here are a few specific examples.

4-1. Extremely small probabilities

Consider the following calculation:

pgamma(1e-100, 3, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
  • R result: -1.6666666666665175e-301
  • High-precision reference value: -1.6666666666666667e-301
  • rStats.js: -1.666666666666667e-301

In this case, the result from rStats.js is much closer to the high-precision reference value.

4-2. Non-central t-distribution calculations

For the non-central t-distribution, there are cases where R fails to correctly calculate extremely small probabilities. For example:

pt(1, 5, ncp = 40)
  • R: 1.009e-303
  • High-precision reference value: 1.0887e-287
  • rStats.js: Matches the high-precision reference value

As shown here, there are instances where simply replicating R's output is insufficient.

Note that the values ​​presented here are taken from the verification examples provided in docs/differences-from-r.md on GitHub.

5. Evaluating quantile functions using a different approach

Quantile functions for probability distributions require a different evaluation method than standard functions. In regions where the cumulative distribution function is very flat, even a tiny difference in probability can lead to a significant discrepancy in the quantile value. Therefore, simply comparing the output against R's results using relative error is not an appropriate approach. rStats.js employs a "backward error" approach, where the result of a quantization function is fed back into the corresponding distribution function for evaluation. In other words, it assesses how closely the value returned by rStats.js—when substituted back into the distribution function—approximates the target probability.

Even if a result differs from that of R, it is considered acceptable provided the backward error is equal to or less than that of R. For discrete distributions, it is also verified that the function returns the smallest integer that satisfies the definition.

6. Verification of Random Number Generation

In addition to statistical functions, rStats.js implements random number generation. It includes a setSeed() function (analogous to R’s set.seed()) and supports various random number generation algorithms, such as Mersenne-Twister and L'Ecuyer-CMRG.

For random number generation, the following aspects are verified:

  • Discrete random numbers and sampling results match those of R.
  • The state of the L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator matches that of R.
  • Continuous random number values ​​fall within an acceptable margin of error.
  • The total count of random numbers consumed matches that of R.

For discrete results, an exact match is required, while for continuous results, the standard is generally a deviation of no more than 1e-12.

Note that for continuous random numbers, results may not match down to the least significant bit; this is due to differences between JavaScript’s Math functions and the mathematical libraries used by the R runtime environment. Such discrepancies are intentional and are considered to be within an acceptable range.

7. Documenting Cases Where Results Differ from R

The goal of rStats.js is not necessarily to achieve an exact match with R in every instance. Because the priority is to ensure mathematically and statistically correct results, the library may occasionally produce outputs that differ from those of R.

Rather than silently excluding such cases from the test suite, these instances are documented as knownDifferences—with the underlying reasons explained—and are made publicly available in the docs/differences-from-r.md file on GitHub. In some cases—such as when R returns NaN or Infinity for undefined results—rStats.js is designed to throw an error instead. By explicitly documenting these discrepancies, we ensure that users are aware of how the library’s behavior differs from that of R.

8. Implementation Supporting Numerical Precision

To achieve this level of precision, rStats.js employs not only standard double-precision floating-point arithmetic but also "Double-Double" arithmetic where necessary. Double-Double arithmetic combines two double-precision floating-point numbers to provide a greater number of significant digits than is otherwise possible.

For instance, this technique is used in calculations such as:

  • Computing the exponent part of exponential functions.
  • Evaluating continued fractions for incomplete beta functions.
  • Evaluating continued fractions for incomplete gamma functions.
  • Asymptotic expansions for large parameters.
  • Operations prone to catastrophic cancellation (loss of precision).

Rather than applying high-precision arithmetic to every calculation, we limit its use to areas where precision is a critical concern, thereby minimizing the impact on the performance of standard calculations.

9. Transparency Regarding Validation Results and Limitations

rStats.js provides full transparency regarding its validation methods and its differences from R via GitHub:

  • Accuracy
  • Differences from R
  • Source code and tests

Within the scope of our validation, no known precision issues have been identified. However, this does not constitute a guarantee of mathematical perfection for all possible input values. Certain precision limitations remain outside the validated range—for example, when dealing with Bessel functions of extremely high order.

We believe that what matters most is not merely claiming high precision, but being transparent about the validation methods used and the inherent limitations of the implementation. ## Conclusion

I believe that JavaScript is not merely a language for developing web applications; it can also serve as a platform for performing reliable statistical computations.

In rStats.js, we verify the accuracy of numerical calculations by using R as a key benchmark, alongside high-precision reference values. Moving forward, I intend to not only expand the range of available statistical methods but also further enhance the reliability and verifiability of these numerical computations.

rStats.js is an open-source project licensed under the MIT License.
GitHub: https://github.com/numero-uno-jpn/rStats.js/

I welcome feedback from developers interested in statistical computing, numerical analysis, and data analysis using JavaScript.

title: Your free model will disappear: tracking OpenRouter's rotating free tier
summary:
Your free model will disappear: tracking OpenRouter's rotating free tier

If you build on OpenRouter's free models, you already know the deal: a model is free today, and one morning it just isn't. The free lineup rotates — models get listed, delisted, or moved to paid — and nothing announces it. Your app doesn't get a deprecation email. It gets a failed API call.

I ran into this the usual way: a hardcoded free model ID in a side project stopped working, and I lost an embarrassing amount of time suspecting my own code before checking whether the model was still free at all. (It wasn't.)

A concrete example

While I was building the tracker described below, it caught this on 2026-10-31:

2026-10-31 13:31 UTC  delisted_free  poolside/laguna-s-2.1:free
2026-10-31 13:31 UTC  delisted_free  poolside/laguna-xs-2.1:free

Two models, gone from the free tier between one check and the next. If either of those was your fallback model, your fallback silently stopped being free.

What I built: FreeModel Radar

FreeModel Radar is a small, boring tracker:

  • A poller queries OpenRouter's public /models endpoint every 30 minutes
  • A model counts as free only when its API pricing is fully $0 — prompt and completion pricing present and zero, and no non-zero charge on any other pricing component
  • Each run diffs the free set against the previous snapshot and records listing/delisting events
  • An empty or sharply shrunken upstream response is refused rather than recorded, so an upstream glitch never wipes the baseline

The outputs are public:

  • Status page — current free list (17 models as of this writing) and recent changes
  • data.json — the machine-readable snapshot behind the page, mirrored in the GitHub repo
  • Free Telegram channel — @freemodelradar posts a daily digest of listing/delisting changes

Using the data instead of hardcoding and praying

The snapshot format is deliberately plain:

{
  "ts": "2026-11-02T14:45:21Z",
  "free_count": 17,

title: Why I Built rStats.js: Bringing Reliable Statistical Computing to JavaScript
summary:
Introduction

I am developing rStats.js, an open-source library for performing statistical analysis in JavaScript.

My goal is to make it easy to access numerically accurate and statistically sound statistical computations from within JavaScript applications.

JavaScript is used not only in web browsers but also in a wide range of other environments, such as Node.js. Meanwhile, R and Python are the dominant languages ​​in the field of statistical analysis; I felt that the options for performing robust statistical computing in JavaScript still had significant room for improvement.

Consequently, I decided to develop a JavaScript library that focuses not just on implementing statistical methods, but also on the precision of numerical calculations and the validity of the underlying algorithms.

Why Develop My Own Instead of Using Existing Statistical Libraries?

There are already several statistical libraries available for JavaScript. I have examined many of these existing libraries while working on my own project.

In doing so, I placed a high priority on the accuracy and verifiability of statistical computations.

Simply having a statistical function implemented is not the same as ensuring that its output is correct under various conditions. In fields like medical research or the analysis of clinical data, even a minor discrepancy in a calculation result could affect how research findings are interpreted.

With rStats.js, I emphasize the following:

  • Adopting statistically sound algorithms.
  • Verifying the precision and stability of numerical computations.
  • Using R’s statistical functions as a key benchmark.
  • Ensuring correct behavior even with boundary values ​​or extreme inputs.
  • Providing an API that is easy to integrate into real-world applications.

Using R as a Key Reference

In the world of statistical analysis, R is a cornerstone.

With rStats.js, I aim to enable similar types of analysis in JavaScript by using R’s functions and statistical methods as a reference.

However, the goal is not to blindly replicate R’s behavior in every instance. We conduct comparative verification against R, while also utilizing high-precision reference values ​​whenever necessary. In cases where our results differ from those produced by R, we prioritize the outcome that is mathematically and statistically correct.

Our focus is not merely on replicating the results of existing software, but on ensuring that the results themselves are accurate.

Bringing Statistical Analysis to JavaScript Applications

A primary goal of rStats.js is to enable the integration of statistical analysis capabilities not only into dedicated statistical software but also into general-purpose web applications and business systems.

Potential use cases include:

  • BI and data analysis tools
  • Survey and research platforms
  • Medical and clinical research systems
  • Educational and learning applications
  • Browser-based statistical analysis tools

Performing statistical calculations directly within a browser offers significant advantages regarding privacy and data management, as it eliminates the need to transmit data to an external server.

Future Outlook

We are currently continuing to expand our range of statistical methods and verify our numerical computations.

Moving forward, we aim to cover a broader spectrum of statistical techniques. We are also committed to enhancing API stability, improving documentation, expanding our test suite, and providing practical code samples—all with the goal of creating a library that developers can rely on with confidence.

Ultimately, we aspire to see this library adopted not only for individual research and study but also integrated into other open-source projects and commercial applications.

The Project

rStats.js is an open-source project released under the MIT License.

GitHub: https://github.com/numero-uno-jpn/rStats.js/

We welcome feedback and contributions from developers looking to perform statistical calculations in JavaScript, as well as from anyone with an interest in statistical algorithms and numerical computation.

Please take a look at the project!
